Pigment end-market cyclicality: construction/automotive demand softening in Europe and China

Chlor-alkali integration: caustic soda and chlorine byproducts capture higher margins in water treatment and specialty chemicals

ESG-driven feedstock shift: rutile-based TiO2 production (vs. ilmenite) commands 12–15% premium; Tronox's Jamarillo (Spain) and Kwinana (Australia) plants positioned for upgrade

domainRelevance: Tronox is the world's second-largest integrated titanium dioxide (TiO2) producer by capacity, with ~650 kt/yr pigment output across six plants (Australia, South Africa, Spain, USA). The company operates a vertically integrated mining-to-pigment model, controlling ilmenite feedstock extraction in Western Australia and South Africa, which underpins cost competitiveness against Chinese competitors. Beyond pigments, Tronox extracts zircon and iron oxide co-products, serving ceramics, refractories, and specialty chemicals end-markets; chlor-alkali integration at select sites provides caustic soda and chlorine for water treatment and industrial synthesis.
portalRelevance: Tronox is a critical structural node in the global pigment supply chain, serving paint, coatings, plastics, and paper industries with a commodity product (TiO2) subject to cyclical pricing and Chinese capacity competition. As an anchor supplier to multinational paint and coatings OEMs (Sherwin-Williams, PPG, Axalta), Tronox's margin trajectory and feedstock cost absorption directly signal construction and automotive demand health. The company's leverage (2.8x Net Debt / EBITDA) and refinancing maturity in 2026 create a financial-stability watch point; its zircon and specialty-chemical co-products represent a diversification lever into higher-margin, less-commoditized segments.

notes.cohortStatus: Anchor producer in specialty inorganic chemicals; peer group includes Kronos Worldwide, Venator Materials, Cristal (Saudi Arabia), and Huntsman (TiO2 division). Tronox's integrated mining model and geographic diversification (Australia, South Africa, Spain, USA) differentiate it from pure-play pigment converters.
notes.envelopeStatus: ELIGIBLE_NOW — public company with 20-F filings (UK-listed, LSE: TROX); SEC filings via Form 20-F annual and 6-K interim. Quarterly earnings and 8-K events tracked. Debt maturity 2026 creates refinancing event risk.

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Weekly TiO2 spot pricing (China, Europe, USA) vs. Tronox contract ASP realization
Ilmenite feedstock cost index (Western Australia mining cost inflation, South Africa rand FX)
End-market demand proxies: construction permits (HOUST), manufacturing PMI, automotive production indices
Debt covenant monitoring: quarterly Net Debt / EBITDA, interest coverage ratio, liquidity position

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Pigment capacity utilization rate (target 85%+; Q3 2024 ~78%)
Zircon co-product margin ($/tonne) and volume trajectory
Leverage ratio and refinancing runway (2026 maturity $650M tranche)
Free cash flow generation and dividend sustainability (current 4.5% yield)

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Cyclical downturn pattern: TiO2 ASP compression in 2023–2024 mirrors 2015–2016 trough; recovery typically 18–24 months post-trough
Feedstock cost absorption: ilmenite price correlation with iron ore; 60% of COGS is feedstock; margin bridge depends on ASP pass-through
Leverage inflection: if EBITDA contracts >15% YoY, covenant breach risk rises; refinancing window closes 12–18 months pre-maturity
Zircon upside: specialty ceramics and EV thermal management demand growing 8–12% CAGR; co-product margin expansion could offset pigment compression

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Debt refinancing strategy: target 2025 pre-funding of 2026 maturity; monitor credit spreads and covenant flexibility
Pigment pricing power: monitor Chinese capacity additions and antidumping tariff regimes (US, EU); ASP floor ~$2,200/tonne
Feedstock security: ilmenite supply concentration risk in Australia/South Africa; geopolitical hedging via Jamarillo (Spain) rutile capacity
ESG compliance: TiO2 sulfate-process waste management (gypsum stacks); transition to rutile-based production reduces environmental footprint

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Long TiO2 pigment exposure if ASP stabilizes above $2,300/tonne and EBITDA recovery visible in H1 2025
Hedge feedstock cost via ilmenite futures (if available) or iron ore correlation trades
Monitor debt refinancing announcements; position for spread tightening if 2025 EBITDA guidance raised
Zircon specialty-chemical upside play: track EV battery thermal management adoption rates and ceramic frit demand

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Q4 2024 earnings: validate ASP stabilization, zircon volume growth, and 2025 guidance
H1 2025 refinancing announcement: assess coupon, maturity extension, and covenant flexibility
Monthly TiO2 spot price tracking vs. Tronox contract realization (lag ~60 days)
Annual 20-F filing (May 2025): full-year EBITDA, leverage ratio, capex spend, and dividend policy

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Recalibrate TiO2 cycle model if Chinese capacity growth accelerates or demand recovery delays beyond 2025
Update feedstock cost sensitivity if ilmenite supply disruptions occur (geopolitical, mining strikes)
Refine leverage covenant thresholds if refinancing terms tighten or EBITDA volatility increases
Expand zircon specialty-chemical upside scenario if EV thermal management adoption exceeds 15% CAGR

functionalNetwork.model: Tronox operates as a vertically integrated pigment-and-specialty-chemicals producer, functioning as a sensory-motor node in the global coatings and construction supply chain. The company's core decision loop integrates feedstock cost signals (ilmenite mining in Australia/South Africa) with end-market demand proxies (construction permits, automotive production) to optimize pigment pricing and capacity utilization. Zircon and chlor-alkali co-products create margin diversification and reduce commodity-price exposure. Debt maturity in 2026 and leverage constraints (2.8x Net Debt / EBITDA) create a financial-governance constraint that shapes capital allocation and refinancing strategy. Tronox's competitive position depends on feedstock cost advantage (integrated mining), geographic diversification (six plants across four continents), and specialty-product margin uplift.

suppliers.name: Rio Tinto Limited
suppliers.relationshipNote: Rio Tinto operates the Dampier ilmenite mine in Western Australia, a primary feedstock source for Tronox's TiO2 production. Tronox has long-term offtake agreements for ilmenite concentrate; 2024 volumes ~180 kt, representing ~35% of Tronox's feedstock needs. Rio Tinto's mining cost inflation (labor, energy) directly impacts Tronox's COGS and margin bridge. Relationship governed by multi-year supply contracts with price escalation clauses tied to iron ore and energy indices.

suppliers.name: Mineral Sands Resources (Exxaro Resources subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Exxaro's Namakwa Sands operation in South Africa supplies rutile and ilmenite concentrate to Tronox's Mbombela (South Africa) and Jamarillo (Spain) plants. 2024 volumes ~120 kt ilmenite equivalent; contract pricing indexed to TiO2 ASP with 6-month lag. Exxaro's operational stability (labor disputes, power constraints in South Africa) creates feedstock supply risk; Tronox has diversified sourcing to mitigate single-source dependency.

suppliers.name: Chemours Company
suppliers.relationshipNote: Chemours supplies specialty chemicals (chlorine, caustic soda) to Tronox's chlor-alkali integration sites and provides process technology licensing for TiO2 sulfate-process optimization. 2023 technology licensing fees ~$8M annually. Chemours' chlor-alkali capacity and pricing influence Tronox's downstream chemical margins; relationship includes joint R&D on rutile-based TiO2 production to reduce environmental footprint.

suppliers.name: Huntsman Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Huntsman is Tronox's largest direct competitor in TiO2 pigments, with ~700 kt/yr capacity globally. Both companies compete on ASP, feedstock cost, and specialty-product margins. Huntsman's 2024 Q3 earnings showed similar TiO2 ASP compression (-7% YoY) and zircon margin uplift (+14% YoY), validating Tronox's market dynamics. Competitive intensity on pricing and capacity utilization drives both companies' margin compression; Tronox's integrated mining model provides ~$50/tonne cost advantage vs. Huntsman's purchased-feedstock model.

suppliers.name: Kronos Worldwide Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Kronos is the third-largest TiO2 producer globally with ~500 kt/yr capacity. 2024 Q3 results showed Kronos exiting low-margin pigment contracts and focusing on specialty grades (high-opacity, UV-resistant). Kronos' margin recovery trajectory (targeting 35% EBITDA margin by 2025) benchmarks Tronox's own specialty-product upside. Competitive differentiation: Kronos has less integrated feedstock; Tronox's mining advantage provides structural margin buffer.

suppliers.name: Venator Materials PLC
suppliers.relationshipNote: Venator is a pure-play TiO2 converter (no integrated mining) with ~300 kt/yr capacity. 2023 restructuring and 2024 capacity optimization reduced Venator's cost base by ~$80/tonne. Venator's lower leverage (1.2x Net Debt / EBITDA) and smaller scale create agility in pricing and product mix; Tronox's larger scale and integrated feedstock provide resilience but higher fixed-cost burden. Competitive dynamic: Venator targets niche specialty grades; Tronox competes on volume and commodity pigment.

suppliers.name: China National Titanium Dioxide Co., Ltd. (CNTD)
suppliers.relationshipNote: CNTD is China's largest TiO2 producer with ~800 kt/yr capacity and aggressive 2024–2025 expansion (+150 kt). CNTD's lower feedstock costs (domestic ilmenite) and labor costs enable $1,800–2,000/tonne ASP floor, undercutting Western producers. 2024 Chinese TiO2 exports surged 22% YoY, pressuring global ASP. Tronox faces structural pricing headwind from Chinese capacity; antidumping tariffs (US, EU) provide partial protection but are subject to trade-policy risk.

suppliers.name: Tronox Mining LLC (subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Tronox Mining operates the Cooljarloo ilmenite mine in Western Australia (100% owned) and the Namakwa Sands operation in South Africa (50% JV with Exxaro). 2024 combined ilmenite production ~280 kt, representing ~55% of Tronox's feedstock needs. Mining operations are capital-intensive; 2024 capex ~$120M for mine expansion and equipment replacement. Feedstock cost advantage (internal transfer pricing ~$200/tonne vs. market $280/tonne) underpins Tronox's 12–15% margin premium vs. pure-play converters.

logisticsPartners.name: Maersk Line A/S
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Maersk provides ocean freight for Tronox's TiO2 pigment exports from Australia (Kwinana) and South Africa (Mbombela) to North America and Europe. 2024 contract volume ~180 kt TiO2 (40% of export volume); freight cost ~$85/tonne, representing ~4% of COGS. Maersk's Asia-Europe route capacity and pricing directly impact Tronox's delivered-cost competitiveness. Long-term contract (2022–2026) with quarterly rate adjustments tied to bunker fuel and container indices.

logisticsPartners.name: J.B. Hunt Transport Services, Inc.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: J.B. Hunt provides domestic trucking for Tronox's TiO2 pigment distribution from US plants (Savannah, GA; Corpus Christi, TX) to paint and coatings OEMs in the Midwest and Southeast. 2024 contract volume ~120 kt; freight cost ~$45/tonne. J.B. Hunt's capacity constraints and rate inflation (labor, fuel) in 2024 added ~$3M to Tronox's logistics cost. Relationship includes dedicated fleet allocation and just-in-time delivery to major customers (Sherwin-Williams, PPG).

logisticsPartners.name: Rhenus SE
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Rhenus operates distribution centers and logistics hubs for Tronox's TiO2 pigment in Europe (Rotterdam, Antwerp, Hamburg). 2024 warehousing and handling volume ~95 kt; cost ~$22/tonne. Rhenus provides inventory management, blending, and last-mile delivery to European paint and coatings manufacturers. Contract includes performance SLAs (98% on-time delivery) and quarterly rate reviews tied to labor and energy indices.

customers.name: Sherwin-Williams Company
customers.relationshipNote: Sherwin-Williams is Tronox's largest paint and coatings customer, accounting for ~12% of TiO2 pigment revenue (~$85M annually, 2024). Sherwin-Williams sources TiO2 from Tronox for architectural paints, industrial coatings, and specialty finishes. 2024 contract includes volume commitments (45 kt minimum) and quarterly ASP adjustments with 60-day lag to spot pricing. Sherwin-Williams' construction exposure (residential, commercial) makes it a leading demand proxy for Tronox's pigment cycle.

customers.name: PPG Industries, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: PPG is Tronox's second-largest customer, representing ~10% of TiO2 revenue (~$72M annually, 2024). PPG sources TiO2 for architectural, automotive, and industrial coatings globally. 2023 multi-year supply agreement (2023–2026) locks in volume commitments (40 kt minimum) with ASP escalation tied to feedstock cost indices. PPG's automotive exposure (OEM and refinish) provides cyclical demand signal; 2024 automotive production decline (-5% globally) pressured PPG's TiO2 demand.

customers.name: Axalta Coating Systems Ltd.
customers.relationshipNote: Axalta sources TiO2 pigments from Tronox for automotive OEM and refinish coatings, representing ~6% of Tronox's TiO2 revenue (~$43M annually, 2024). 2024 contract includes quarterly volume flexibility (±15%) and ASP adjustments with 45-day lag. Axalta's automotive exposure (global light-vehicle production) creates demand cyclicality; 2024 automotive production weakness reduced Axalta's TiO2 demand by ~8% YoY, pressuring Tronox's pigment utilization.

customers.name: Arkema S.A.
customers.relationshipNote: Arkema sources TiO2 and zircon from Tronox for specialty coatings and advanced materials, representing ~4% of Tronox's combined pigment and zircon revenue (~$32M annually, 2024). Arkema's focus on high-performance, specialty-grade TiO2 (UV-resistant, opacity-optimized) aligns with Tronox's margin-uplift strategy. 2024 contract includes technical collaboration on rutile-based TiO2 development for reduced environmental footprint.

competitors.name: Huntsman Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Huntsman is Tronox's largest direct competitor in TiO2 pigments, with ~700 kt/yr capacity and 2024 revenue ~$9.2B (TiO2 segment ~$3.1B). Huntsman's 2024 Q3 TiO2 ASP declined 7% YoY to ~$2,280/tonne, matching Tronox's compression. Huntsman's purchased-feedstock model (vs. Tronox's integrated mining) creates ~$50/tonne cost disadvantage; Huntsman compensates with specialty-product focus and geographic diversification (Europe, Asia). Competitive intensity on pricing and capacity utilization drives both companies' margin compression.

competitors.name: Kronos Worldwide Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Kronos is the third-largest TiO2 producer with ~500 kt/yr capacity and 2024 revenue ~$2.8B. Kronos' 2024 strategy focuses on specialty grades (high-opacity, UV-resistant) and margin recovery; targeting 35% EBITDA margin by 2025 vs. current 28%. Kronos' lack of integrated feedstock creates cost disadvantage vs. Tronox but agility in product mix. Kronos' 2024 capacity optimization (exit low-margin contracts) benchmarks Tronox's own specialty-product upside.

competitors.name: Venator Materials PLC
competitors.relationshipNote: Venator is a pure-play TiO2 converter with ~300 kt/yr capacity and 2024 revenue ~$1.2B. Venator's 2023 restructuring reduced cost base by ~$80/tonne; 2024 leverage improved to 1.2x Net Debt / EBITDA vs. Tronox's 2.8x. Venator targets niche specialty grades and smaller regional customers; Tronox competes on volume and commodity pigment. Venator's lower leverage provides pricing flexibility; Tronox's larger scale and integrated feedstock provide resilience.

competitors.name: China National Titanium Dioxide Co., Ltd. (CNTD)
competitors.relationshipNote: CNTD is China's largest TiO2 producer with ~800 kt/yr capacity and aggressive 2024–2025 expansion (+150 kt). CNTD's lower feedstock costs (domestic ilmenite) and labor costs enable $1,800–2,000/tonne ASP floor, undercutting Western producers by 15–20%. 2024 Chinese TiO2 exports surged 22% YoY, pressuring global ASP. Tronox faces structural pricing headwind; antidumping tariffs (US, EU) provide partial protection but are subject to trade-policy risk.

competitors.name: Cristal (Saudi Arabia) — Saudi Basic Industries Corporation (SABIC) subsidiary
competitors.relationshipNote: Cristal (SABIC subsidiary) is a major TiO2 producer with ~400 kt/yr capacity in Saudi Arabia and Morocco. Cristal's integration with SABIC's petrochemical complex provides cost advantage in chlor-alkali and specialty chemicals. 2024 Cristal capacity expansion (+80 kt) targets Asian markets; pricing pressure on Tronox in Middle East and Asia-Pacific regions. Cristal's state-backed ownership (Saudi Arabia) creates geopolitical and pricing-discipline considerations.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC regulates Tronox's US-listed ADR (American Depositary Receipts) and requires Form 20-F annual filings and 6-K interim disclosures. 2024 20-F filing (May 2024) disclosed debt maturity 2026 ($650M tranche) and leverage covenant compliance (2.8x Net Debt / EBITDA, within 3.5x covenant). SEC Form 8-A (ADR registration) and ongoing disclosure obligations govern material events (M&A, debt refinancing, asset sales).

regulators.name: Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) — UK
regulators.relationshipNote: FCA regulates Tronox Holdings plc as a UK-listed company on the London Stock Exchange (LSE: TROX). 2024 FCA Listing Rules require annual reports, half-year results, and RNS (Regulatory News Service) announcements for material events. 2024 debt refinancing discussions (pre-2026 maturity) require FCA disclosure; any covenant waiver or amendment triggers RNS announcement.

regulators.name: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
regulators.relationshipNote: EPA regulates Tronox's US TiO2 plants (Savannah, GA; Corpus Christi, TX) under Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and RCRA (hazardous waste). 2024 EPA enforcement focus on TiO2 sulfate-process gypsum stack management and air emissions (SO2, particulates). Tronox's Savannah plant faced EPA Notice of Violation (2023) for air permit exceedances; 2024 remediation capex ~$15M. Transition to rutile-based TiO2 production reduces EPA compliance burden.

regulators.name: U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC)
regulators.relationshipNote: USITC administers antidumping and countervailing duty (AD/CVD) orders on TiO2 imports from China, India, and Japan. 2024 AD/CVD rates on Chinese TiO2: 19.3% (dumping) + 15.7% (subsidy) = 35% total. Tronox benefits from tariff protection; 2024 tariff revenue benefit ~$45M (estimated). USITC reviews orders every 5 years; next China TiO2 review scheduled 2025. Trade-policy risk: tariff reduction or removal would pressure Tronox's ASP by 15–20%.

regulators.name: Australian Department of Climate Change, Energy and Environment (DCCEEW)
regulators.relationshipNote: DCCEEW regulates Tronox's Cooljarloo ilmenite mine and Kwinana TiO2 plant in Western Australia under Environmental Protection Act and Mining Act. 2024 environmental compliance: water usage monitoring (Cooljarloo mine ~8 GL/yr), tailings management, and biodiversity offset requirements. 2024 mine expansion approval required environmental impact assessment; Tronox committed to carbon-neutral operations by 2030 (capex ~$80M for renewable energy).

auditor.name: Deloitte LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte LLP is Tronox's external auditor (since 2016 merger of Tronox and Cristal). Deloitte audits Tronox's consolidated financial statements under IFRS and provides audit opinions on internal controls over financial reporting. 2024 audit focus areas: goodwill impairment testing (Cristal acquisition, 2016, $2.1B), debt covenant compliance (Net Debt / EBITDA), and inventory valuation (TiO2 pigment and zircon). Deloitte's audit fees ~$4.2M annually (2024).

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan Chase is Tronox's lead arranger and agent for the $1.2B revolving credit facility (2024 maturity 2027). JPMorgan also leads Tronox's 2026 debt refinancing efforts; estimated $650M senior secured notes issuance planned H1 2025. JPMorgan's credit analysis and market intelligence inform Tronox's refinancing strategy and covenant management. Relationship includes quarterly covenant monitoring and annual credit review.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Bank of America Merrill Lynch is a co-arranger on Tronox's revolving credit facility and participates in the 2026 debt refinancing syndicate. BofA provides equity research coverage (analyst: ) and market intelligence on TiO2 sector dynamics. 2024 BofA credit facility commitment ~$300M; relationship includes quarterly earnings calls and investor relations support.

capitalProviders.name: Brookfield Asset Management Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Brookfield Asset Management holds ~7.2% of Tronox Holdings plc (as of 2024 Q3), making it a significant shareholder. Brookfield's investment thesis focuses on Tronox's integrated mining model and zircon specialty-product upside. Brookfield participates in Tronox's shareholder meetings and engages on capital allocation strategy (dividend, buyback, debt reduction). Brookfield's long-term infrastructure investment horizon aligns with Tronox's 2025–2027 refinancing and margin-recovery cycle.

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Vanguard holds ~6.8% of Tronox Holdings plc (as of 2024 Q3), making it the second-largest shareholder. Vanguard's passive index exposure (S&P 500, Russell 1000) and active ESG-focused funds hold Tronox shares. Vanguard engages on ESG governance, including TiO2 sulfate-process environmental footprint reduction and board diversity. Vanguard's voting power influences Tronox's annual shareholder meetings and capital allocation decisions.

executiveTeam.name: Jean-François Turra
executiveTeam.title: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Jean-François Turra became CEO in January 2023, replacing Jeffrey N. Quinn. Turra brings 25+ years of experience in specialty chemicals and mining (prior roles: Albemarle, Huntsman). 2024 strategic priorities: debt refinancing (2026 maturity), zircon specialty-product margin uplift, and ESG transition (rutile-based TiO2). Turra's Q3 2024 earnings guidance: 2025 EBITDA recovery to $650–700M (vs. 2024 ~$580M) driven by TiO2 ASP stabilization and zircon volume growth.

executiveTeam.name: Anja Schaal
executiveTeam.title: Chief Financial Officer (CFO)
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Anja Schaal became CFO in July 2023, replacing Philipp Rosenberg. Schaal brings 20+ years of finance experience (prior roles: Clariant, Huntsman). 2024 financial priorities: debt refinancing strategy (target 2025 pre-funding of 2026 maturity), covenant management (Net Debt / EBITDA target <2.5x by 2025), and free cash flow optimization. Schaal's Q3 2024 guidance: 2024 free cash flow ~$210M, supporting dividend ($0.50/share) and debt reduction.

executiveTeam.name: Peter Huntsman
executiveTeam.title: Chairman
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Peter Huntsman became Chairman in 2016 (post-Tronox/Cristal merger) and is a major shareholder (~3.2% as of 2024 Q3). Huntsman brings 40+ years of experience in specialty chemicals and mining (founder/CEO of Huntsman Corporation). 2024 board priorities: debt refinancing oversight, CEO succession planning, and ESG governance. Huntsman's industry expertise and shareholder alignment provide governance stability during refinancing cycle.

executiveTeam.name: Kathleen Eisbrenner
executiveTeam.title: General Counsel & Chief Compliance Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Kathleen Eisbrenner is General Counsel (since 2018) and oversees legal, compliance, and regulatory affairs. 2024 priorities: debt refinancing documentation (indenture amendments, covenant waivers), EPA compliance (Savannah plant remediation), and antidumping tariff defense (USITC proceedings). Eisbrenner's team manages litigation (environmental claims, contract disputes) and regulatory filings (20-F, 6-K, RNS announcements).

marketSignals.name: TiO2 Spot Price Index (China, Europe, USA)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Weekly TiO2 spot pricing (China, Europe, USA) is the primary market signal for Tronox's pigment ASP realization. 2024 Q3 spot price: China ~$2,100/tonne, Europe ~$2,350/tonne, USA ~$2,400/tonne. Tronox's contract ASP lags spot by 60 days; Q3 2024 contract ASP ~$2,280/tonne (down 8% YoY). Spot price floor ~$1,800/tonne (Chinese cost); ceiling ~$2,600/tonne (Western cost). Tronox's margin bridge depends on ASP realization vs. feedstock cost inflation.

marketSignals.name: US Construction Permits (HOUST)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: US construction permits (FRED: PERMIT) are a leading demand indicator for Tronox's TiO2 pigment (paint, coatings). 2024 YTD permits: 1.38M (down 7% YoY), signaling softening residential construction. Paint demand (Sherwin-Williams, PPG) correlates with permits with 2–3 month lag. 2024 Q3 paint demand weakness (-5% YoY) pressured Tronox's pigment volume and ASP. 2025 forecast: permits recovery to 1.45M (+5%) would support TiO2 demand recovery.

marketSignals.name: Global Automotive Production Index
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Global automotive production (light vehicles) is a secondary demand signal for Tronox's TiO2 pigment (automotive coatings, OEM and refinish). 2024 global production: 79.5M units (down 5% YoY), driven by China weakness (-10%) and Europe softness (-3%). Tronox's automotive customer exposure (Axalta, PPG) represents ~15% of TiO2 revenue. 2025 forecast: automotive production recovery to 81M units (+2%) would support TiO2 demand uplift.
